• 2021: 4 Black NYC firefighters with PFB were unsuccessful obtaining medical accommodation against a clean-shaven mandate (Jiang 2023).
• Limited dermatology access in SOC populations → delayed presentation, more advanced disease at first visit, more PIH and scarring sequelae.

OCCUPATIONAL CONTEXT (military, firefighter, police, food service): These patients are caught between regulation and biology. Coaching language should validate this conflict — 'this is a structural problem, not a personal failure' — while providing the maximal-mitigation technique stack (clippers + Nd:YAG + glycolic + eflornithine + BPO/clinda topical).

IMPLICATIONS FOR RR AI REVIEW:
• Any beard-area papular complaint in Fitz IV-VI → assume PFB even without textbook erythema.
• Plan should include the FULL updated technique stack (multiblade + foam + lukewarm water + no skin tension + shave with grain + post-shave moisturizer).
• For occupational cases: offer hair clippers as a regulation-compatible alternative when full shaving cessation is impossible.
• Add glycolic acid (alpha hydroxy) to the regimen — it targets the curl bond, not just inflammation.
• Discuss Nd:YAG + eflornithine combination for definitive plans, with frank cost/access discussion.
• Validate the occupational and career stakes — do not treat PFB as a cosmetic concern.

library_docs.title: Weight Reduction with GLP-1 Agonists and Paths for Discontinuation While Maintaining Weight Loss — Reiss, Gulkarov, Lau, Klek, Srivastava, Renna, De Leon (Biomolecules 2025)
library_docs.source: Reiss AB, Gulkarov S, Lau R, Klek SP, Srivastava A, Renna HA, De Leon J. Weight Reduction with GLP-1 Agonists and Paths for Discontinuation While Maintaining Weight Loss. Biomolecules 2025; 15: 408. DOI: 10.3390/biom15030408. NYU Grossman Long Island School of Medicine. Open access CC BY. Published March 13, 2025.
library_docs.summary:
Comprehensive 2025 peer-reviewed review of GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight loss, their adverse effects, and the open problem of discontinuation without weight regain. CRITICAL for any wellness assessment of a patient currently or previously on a GLP-1 — these drugs affect the skin, hair, body composition, and long-term metabolism in ways patients are rarely warned about.

EFFICACY: GLP-1 agonists reduce body weight 15-25% on average at ~1 year. Tirzepatide (dual GLP-1/GIP agonist) shows up to 22% loss over 1 year. Mechanism: mimic endogenous GLP-1, an intestinal hormone regulating glucose metabolism and satiety. Effect is predominantly on energy INTAKE (reduced appetite), not energy expenditure.

BOXED WARNING: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma OR multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN2). Do NOT use in these patients. Niya should always screen this in intake before any GLP-1 conversation.

COMMON GI ADVERSE EFFECTS and mitigation:
• Nausea/vomiting — gradual dose increase, small meals, anti-emetics.
• Diarrhea — hydration, low-fiber foods, reduce dairy, coffee, alcohol.
• Constipation — physical activity, hydration, ample fiber.
• Pancreatitis (rare) — discontinue + standard treatment.
• Gastroparesis with anesthesia — discontinue at least 1 week prior to any procedure.

SKIN AND COSMETIC EFFECTS (HIGHLY RELEVANT TO AESTHETIC PRACTICE):
• 'OZEMPIC FACE': Rapid facial fat-pad depletion causes hollowed cheeks, more prominent wrinkles, and pronounced eye bags. Premature facial aging. Patients often present asking about fillers or facelift after starting GLP-1. Cosmetic options listed in the paper: facelift, dermal fillers, autologous fat transfer (Humphrey 2023, Ruff 2024).
• GLP-1-ASSOCIATED ALOPECIA: Hair thinning + diffuse hair loss documented (Desai 2023). Mitigation in the paper: change to a different GLP-1 medication, topical hair loss treatments (minoxidil 5%). Most patients don't connect their hair shedding to the drug — ASK directly: 'When did the hair changes start, and was it around the time you started semaglutide/tirzepatide?'
• Both 'Ozempic face' and GLP-1 alopecia are CLASS EFFECTS of rapid weight loss, not specific to one drug — they are seen with bariatric surgery and aggressive caloric restriction as well. Same underlying mechanism: rate of fat/protein loss exceeds the body's ability to remodel cosmetically.

LEAN BODY MASS / SARCOPENIA RISK (the most under-discussed concern):
• STEP 1 trial of semaglutide: significant loss of total lean body mass. Confirmed by other investigators (Wilding 2021, Neeland 2024). Tirzepatide shows similar lean mass loss.
• Particularly dangerous in patients with sarcopenic obesity (muscle:fat mismatch already present).
• MITIGATION (this is where wellness coaching can change outcomes):
   - RESISTANCE TRAINING — non-negotiable. 2-3x/week minimum, full-body, progressive overload. Compound lifts > isolation.
   - ADEQUATE PROTEIN — typical recommendation 1.2-1.6 g/kg ideal body weight/day, distributed across meals (20-40g/meal). Many GLP-1 patients eat very little overall due to reduced appetite, so per-meal protein content matters more than ever.
   - Adequate calories despite reduced appetite — under-eating drives lean mass loss faster.
   - Vitamin D, omega-3, creatine monohydrate (5g/day) — adjuncts that support muscle.

OTHER ADVERSE EFFECTS:
• Increased heart rate — benign, no associated arrhythmias.
• Headaches, dizziness, hypoglycemia, injection site reactions — lower incidence.
• Rapid weight loss-associated biliary disease.

WEIGHT REGAIN AFTER DISCONTINUATION (the open problem):
• STEP 1 extension trial: substantial weight regain after discontinuation, with reversal of cardiometabolic improvements.
• SURMOUNT-4 tirzepatide trial: similar pattern.
• Drivers of weight regain: hypometabolism + hyperphagia in the weight-reduced state — the body defends its set point.
• Mitigation strategies under investigation:
   - GLP-1 tapering (lower dose or prolonged dosing intervals) — emerging, limited evidence.
   - 'Drug holidays' — almost no literature; not currently recommended without supervision.
   - Behavioral + nutritional + structured physical activity + peer support — multi-pronged approach is the only durable path identified.
   - Switching to a different anti-obesity medication (e.g., Contrave) at discontinuation — under study.
   - Bariatric surgery has the most durable weight loss long-term (~22% sustained at 20 years), but with its own risks.

IMPLICATIONS FOR RR AI REVIEW + WELLNESS COACHING:
• Any patient who reports being on Ozempic/Wegovy/Mounjaro/Zepbound/semaglutide/tirzepatide should have their wellness plan address: resistance training, protein adequacy, hydration, GI side effect management, and facial volume/hair changes if relevant to their concern.
• Patients with 'Ozempic face' concern should be counseled that this is a structural class effect, not a personal failing. Cosmetic options exist (filler, autologous fat transfer) but slowing the rate of weight loss + protein/training adequacy can prevent some of it.
• Patients with new diffuse hair loss who are on a GLP-1 should be told this association is real and that medication switching + minoxidil 5% are options.
• Patients planning to STOP a GLP-1 should be set up with a multi-pronged maintenance plan BEFORE discontinuation, not after weight regain has started.
• Screen for medullary thyroid carcinoma family history before any GLP-1 conversation.
• Sarcopenia mitigation = resistance training + protein. This is the single most actionable wellness lever and is severely under-emphasized in primary-care GLP-1 conversations.
• Wellness coaching language: 'GLP-1s are a powerful tool, not a destination. The work we do alongside them — building muscle, protecting your skin, planning for what comes after — is what makes the weight loss last.'

library_docs.title: Through the Haze: What Clinicians Can Do to Address Youth Vaping — Hadland, Chadi (Journal of Adolescent Health 2020)
library_docs.source: Hadland SE, Chadi N. Through the Haze: What Clinicians Can Do to Address Youth Vaping. J Adolesc Health. 2020 Jan;66(1):10-14. DOI: 10.1016/j.jadohealth.2019.10.009. PMC NIHMS preprint. Boston Medical Center / Sainte-Justine University Hospital Centre.
library_docs.summary:
Peer-reviewed clinical commentary from the Journal of Adolescent Health on screening, counseling, and treating youth (adolescents + young adults) for vaping/e-cigarette nicotine addiction. THE key clinical reference for any RR client under 25 who vapes, or any parent client seeking guidance for their teen.

WHY THIS MATTERS: Vaping disproportionately affects youth. JUUL and pod-mod devices deliver high concentrations of nicotine — a 5%-nicotine JUUL pod delivers about as much nicotine as a PACK OF 20 COMBUSTIBLE CIGARETTES. Many youth do not realize they are even consuming nicotine. Vaping increases risk of transition to combustible cigarettes AND cannabis, drives nicotine addiction in developing brains, and carries acute risks (EVALI lung injury, seizures).

SCREENING — adapt validated tools to vaping:
• S2BI (Screening to Brief Intervention) — 1-question annual screen, freely available.
• BSTAD (Brief Screener for Tobacco, Alcohol, and other Drugs) — freely available.
• Hooked on Nicotine Checklist (HONC) — validated for adolescents, detects nicotine withdrawal + cravings.
• USE YOUTH TERMINOLOGY: 'e-cigarettes, pods, mods, vape pens, JUUL, disposables' — NOT 'tobacco' (youth don't think of vaping as tobacco).
• Follow-up questions when use is disclosed: what they're vaping (nicotine vs THC vs flavoring), where they buy it (illicit market = EVALI risk), how often they replace pods, daily use pattern.
• Heavy use marker: a 5% JUUL pod ~ 1 pack of cigarettes — ask 'how many pods per week?'
• Red flags for DSM-5 substance use disorder: loss of control, social impairment, unsafe use, tolerance, withdrawal.

COUNSELING — the 5 A's framework adapted for youth vaping:
1. ASK — every visit. 'Do you vape? Use pods, mods, JUUL, disposables?'
2. ADVISE — concise, youth-tailored, NOT scare-tactic. Cover EVALI, seizures, addiction risk.
3. ASSESS — strength-based motivational interviewing. Help youth identify THEIR pros (social, mood/anxiety coping) and cons (cost, addiction, withdrawal) of vaping.
4. ASSIST — work with youth on quit date if motivated, OR harm reduction (reduce frequency/intensity) if not yet ready. Motivational interviewing continues regardless.
5. ARRANGE — close follow-up surrounding quit date. Each unsuccessful attempt increases the likelihood that the next one succeeds.

THE 'ABSTINENCE CHALLENGE': Many youth believe they can stop anytime but choose not to. A short stop-for-X-days challenge often reveals dependence and shifts motivation.

BEHAVIORAL SUPPORTS:
• Individual or group counseling, CBT, mindfulness.
• Phone/text quit lines: in US, My Life My Quit and the quitSTART app.
• Regular physical exercise + prosocial activities (NOT activities with peers who vape).
• Distraction techniques: fidget toys, stress balls, toothpicks.
• Family involvement when possible — parents can hold devices, reinforce change, support adherence to behavioral + pharmacological plans, provide transportation/money support.
• Youth resistant to family involvement: keep working on it at follow-ups, do not force.

PHARMACOTHERAPY (REFERRAL TERRITORY for an RN wellness coach — this is prescribing scope):
• NICOTINE REPLACEMENT THERAPY (NRT): recommended for adolescents under 18 who are quitting. Combination = long-acting patch + short-acting gum or lozenge for breakthrough cravings. AVOID short-acting nicotine inhalers or oral/nasal sprays in youth (misuse risk, reinforcing effects).
• BUPROPION: limited data under 18, may be considered with behavioral interventions.
• VARENICLINE: NOT recommended under 17.
• NO effective medications for cannabis (THC vape) withdrawal in youth.

ACUTE HARMS to flag for urgent medical evaluation:
• EVALI (e-cigarette/vaping-associated lung injury) — cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, GI symptoms, fever. Higher risk with illicit/black-market THC products. → urgent ED or PCP evaluation.
• Vaping-associated seizures — direct referral to neurology + cessation.
• Severe withdrawal symptoms during cessation attempts.

IMPLICATIONS FOR RR (scope-of-practice notes for Niya):
• RR's smoking cessation program intake already captures vape as a type. For clients under 25 who select vape, anchor the plan in this Hadland 2020 framework.
• Niya CAN: screen with adapted S2BI/BSTAD/HONC; deliver 5 A's counseling; coach behavioral supports; recommend OTC NRT patch + gum/lozenge combo (NOT inhaler/spray); facilitate family involvement; refer for Rx pharmacotherapy or acute symptoms.
• Niya should NOT: prescribe bupropion/varenicline (refer to PCP or adolescent medicine); attempt to treat acute EVALI symptoms (→ urgent care).
• For teens under 18: parental consent ALREADY required by RR intake — leverage that conversation to enroll the family in the treatment plan.
• Document quit date + 1, 4, 7, 30, 90 day milestones — relapse early in attempts is normal; positive framing matters.
• Coaching language: 'Vaping was designed to be hard to quit — that's the chemistry, not your willpower. We're going to work with that, not against it.'

library_docs.title: Alopecia areata — Pratt, King, Messenger, Christiano, Sundberg (Nat Rev Dis Primers, 2017) — Definitive Disease Primer
library_docs.source: Pratt CH, King LE Jr, Messenger AG, Christiano AM, Sundberg JP. Alopecia areata. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2017 Mar 16;3:17011. doi:10.1038/nrdp.2017.11. PMID: 28300084. Peer-reviewed, 207 references. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrdp.2017.11
library_docs.summary:
AUTHORITATIVE SOURCE — Nature Reviews Disease Primers, 2017. Use as the foundational citation any time Radiant Revive content touches alopecia areata (AA). Comprehensive disease overview from epidemiology through emerging therapeutics.

KEY POINTS FOR RR USE:

EPIDEMIOLOGY: ~2% lifetime prevalence (worldwide, all populations). Slight female predominance. Bimodal incidence with one peak in childhood/adolescence and another in 30s–40s. ~20% present before age 18.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY (the testable mechanism): Hair follicles enjoy 'immune privilege' during anagen (active growth) — they down-regulate MHC class I/II and locally suppress NK cells. In AA, this privilege COLLAPSES. CD8+NKG2D+ T-cells recognize follicular self-antigens, infiltrate the peribulbar region ('swarm of bees' on histology), and arrest anagen. IFN-γ is the central cytokine. JAK1/JAK2/JAK3-STAT signaling downstream — explains why JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, ruxolitinib, and later baricitinib/ritlecitinib) work. Hair follicle stem cells are NOT destroyed — explains why regrowth is possible even after years.

GENETICS: GWAS identifies multiple loci including HLA region (strongest), ULBP3 / ULBP6 (NKG2D ligands), CTLA4, IL-2/IL-21, IL-2RA, Eos. Family history present in ~10–42%. Twin concordance higher in monozygotic. Shared genetic architecture with other autoimmune disease (T1D, vitiligo, RA, celiac).

DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS:
• Clinical: smooth, round/oval patches; exclamation-mark hairs; positive pull test at active edge; preserved follicular ostia.
• Dermoscopy (high yield): yellow dots, black dots, exclamation marks, broken hairs, short vellus regrowth, tapered hairs.
• Histopathology when needed: peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate, pigment incontinence, miniaturized follicles, catagen/telogen shift, preserved follicular architecture.
• Nail exam: pitting (10–66%), trachyonychia, ridging, red lunulae — correlates with severity.

COMORBIDITIES TO SCREEN: thyroid disease (most common — TSH/T4/TPO), vitiligo, atopy/atopic dermatitis, T1D, celiac, RA, psoriasis. Anxiety/depression elevated and clinically significant.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS (Box 1 in paper — RR cribs from this for Reva triage logic): scarring vs non-scarring is the primary fork.
   NON-SCARRING: AA, androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium, anagen effluvium, trichotillomania, traction alopecia (early), tinea capitis.
   SCARRING (cicatricial — refer to dermatology): CCCA, frontal fibrosing alopecia, lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus, folliculitis decalvans, dissecting cellulitis.

TREATMENT (per primer; updated 2024 with FDA approvals post-publication):
• Limited disease (<50% scalp): topical/intralesional corticosteroids, minoxidil, anthralin.
• Extensive disease (>50%, totalis, universalis): topical immunotherapy (DPCP, SADBE), systemic corticosteroids (pulsed, rebound risk), methotrexate.
• Severe/refractory: JAK inhibitors — strong RCT evidence in the primer and validated by subsequent FDA approvals (baricitinib 2022, ritlecitinib 2023). Class warnings: infection, lipids, CBC, malignancy/MACE.
• Cosmetic prosthetics + psychosocial support are not adjuncts — they are PART of treatment.

PROGNOSTIC FACTORS (worse): pediatric onset, extensive disease, ophiasis pattern, nail involvement, atopy, family history, autoimmune comorbidity. Spontaneous regrowth in ~50% of limited adult-onset patchy AA within 12 months without treatment.

QUALITY OF LIFE: DLQI scores comparable to severe psoriasis. Bullying in pediatric AA is well-documented. Major depression and social phobia prevalence elevated.

C3H/HeJ MOUSE MODEL: spontaneous AA-like disease — primary research model for translational work. RR doesn't use this but worth knowing for SBIR grant context (NIH NIAMS reviewers will recognize it).

WHEN TO CITE IN RR CONTENT:
• Provider Portal AA case (this library entry).
• Reva hair-loss scripted dialogue (cite as evidence base for differential triage).
• Patient-facing education page on AA (cite as authoritative source).
• SBIR Research Strategy / Bibliography (peer-reviewed primer with 207 references is exactly the kind of citation reviewers expect for clinical context).
• Niya Clinical Knowledge docx series (Niya-Clinical-Knowledge-Alopecia-Areata.docx companion file).

FULL SOURCE FILE: /sessions/.../uploads/Alopecia.pdf — 1.2 MB scientific paper, on file in Radiant Revive uploads.

2025 comprehensive 20-year retrospective review of skin of color (SOC) dermatology by Susan C. Taylor, MD (Penn Med Dermatology) — the senior author who wrote the field-defining 2002 paper that launched SOC dermatology as a formal subspecialty. Published in JAAD Reviews. Essential reference doc for any SOC-focused clinical decision support.

SCOPE: The review synthesizes 20 years of advancements across (a) structural + biological characteristics of skin and hair in SOC populations; (b) inflammatory cutaneous diseases; (c) alopecias and other scalp diseases (including CCCA); (d) disorders of nail pigmentation; and (e) cosmetic interventions in SOC. Closes with a forward look at personalized medicine, genetic research, and artificial intelligence as the anticipated next frontier for SOC-specific care.

Desir/Taylor 2025 complements both with (1) the 20-year historical arc showing what has changed and what has not; (2) Susan Taylor's authority as the field's founding voice; and (3) an explicit call for AI + personalized medicine as the next 20 years of SOC dermatology — which is exactly the frame the Radiant Revive platform lives inside.

Nature Medicine. 2024. doi:10.1038/s41591-023-02728-3. Matt Groh, PhD — Northwestern Kellogg / Human-AI Collaboration Lab. Curated for Radiant Revive by Dr. Groh 2026-07-15. Companion Kellogg Insight: https://insight.kellogg.northwestern.edu/article/what-happens-when-we-give-doctors-an-ai-assistant
library_docs.summary:
DEFINITIVE EMPIRICAL STUDY of physician-AI collaboration in dermatology, stratified by patient skin tone. Curated by Dr. Matt Groh (lead author) as a follow-up reference for Radiant Revive's methodology.

KEY CLINICAL POINTS THE AI SHOULD APPLY:

1. AI DECISION SUPPORT NARROWS BUT DOES NOT FULLY CLOSE THE FITZPATRICK ACCURACY GAP — Physicians using AI assistance improve diagnostic accuracy overall, but the accuracy gap between light-skinned (Fitzpatrick I-III) and dark-skinned (Fitzpatrick IV-VI) patients persists even with AI support. This is the empirical foundation for Radiant Revive's dual-axis fairness measurement architecture.

2. HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP IS BETTER THAN AI ALONE — Neither AI nor physician alone matches the combined physician+AI performance. This validates the Radiant Revive Provider Portal design: AI generates candidate assessments, RN reviews before delivery. The paper is empirical evidence for the human-in-the-loop patent claim.

3. AI-ASSISTED DIAGNOSIS DOES NOT REDUCE PHYSICIAN AUTONOMY OR ACCOUNTABILITY — Physicians retained decision authority; AI provided candidates and confidence estimates. Framing matters for FDA regulatory pathway (Clinical Decision Support classification).

4. THE ACCURACY GAP IS BEHAVIORAL, NOT PURELY ALGORITHMIC — Even when the underlying AI has similar accuracy across skin tones, physicians' USE of the AI (which suggestions they follow, which they override) is influenced by skin tone. This is a new axis of bias distinct from model bias itself.

5. STUDY DESIGN AS METHODOLOGY REFERENCE — Deep-dive the study's experimental design when Radiant Revive plans its own physician-AI validation study for FDA pre-submission.

SBIR/PATENT REFERENCE USE:
- Cite in SBIR Preliminary Data section as empirical justification for Radiant Revive's AI-plus-nurse workflow.
- Cite in FDA pre-submission as basis for Clinical Decision Support (not autonomous diagnostic) classification.
- Cite in JDNA follow-up publications on the physician/nurse + AI collaboration paradigm.
- Cite in patent prosecution response if asked about clinical validation frameworks.

RELATED COAUTHOR NOTE:
Roxana Daneshjou (Stanford) is a coauthor. She is also lead author of Daneshjou et al. 2022 — the paper documenting the original 27-36% ROC-AUC gap that Radiant Revive already cites. These two papers form a citation cluster: gap identification (2022) → gap-narrowing intervention with AI (2024) → Radiant Revive's methodology to further close it.

SCOPE OF PRACTICE: Niya's methodology is nurse-led, not physician-led. This paper's physician-AI framework informs how Radiant Revive's nurse-AI workflow should be structured — the human-in-the-loop principle transfers. Nurses remain within RN/FNP scope of practice; AI assists rather than replaces clinical judgment.

library_docs.source: Groh M, Harris C, Daneshjou R, Badri O, Koochek A. Towards transparency in dermatology image datasets with experts, crowds, and an algorithm. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction. 2022;6(CSCW2):Article 458. doi:10.1145/3555634. Matt Groh, PhD — Northwestern Kellogg. Curated for Radiant Revive by Dr. Groh 2026-07-15. Replication code: https://github.com/mattgroh/fitzpatrick17k
library_docs.summary:
METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATION for how skin-tone labels are constructed and validated in dermatology image datasets. Curated by Dr. Matt Groh as a follow-up reference. Directly informs Radiant Revive's Measurement Protocol v1.1 dual-axis stratification decision.

KEY METHODOLOGICAL POINTS THE AI SHOULD APPLY:

1. THREE LABELING SOURCES, THREE DIFFERENT ANSWERS — Fitzpatrick labels from (a) board-certified dermatologists, (b) crowdsourced non-expert workers, and (c) individual typology angle algorithm applied to image pixels DO NOT agree on the same images. Any dataset that treats labels from one source as ground truth inherits that source's biases.

2. INTER-RATER RELIABILITY IS LOWER FOR DARKER SKIN TONES — Consistent finding across labeling methods: Fitzpatrick brackets V-VI have LOWER agreement across raters than I-II or III-IV. This is a critical fairness caveat for any Fitzpatrick-stratified analysis (including Radiant Revive's).

3. THIS IS WHY FITZPATRICK 17K USES CROWDSOURCED LABELS — The paper documents the labeling protocol used to construct the Fitzpatrick 17k dataset itself. The 'undetermined' (-1) values in Fitzpatrick 17k that Radiant Revive filters in the sandbox loader are cases where crowdsourced raters could not agree.

4. IMPLICATIONS FOR RADIANT REVIVE:
   - Radiant Revive's dual-axis architecture (FST + MST as independent axes, never merged) is empirically justified by this paper: even within a single axis, labels are noisy; combining axes without care would compound the noise.
   - Any Radiant Revive publication citing Fitzpatrick-stratified performance MUST cite this paper as the methodological foundation for how the labels were derived.
   - Consider adding an 'annotator agreement' or 'label confidence' field to Radiant Revive's data schema when curating proprietary training data in the future.

5. ALGORITHMIC LABEL ESTIMATION (individual typology angle from image pixels) IS AN OPTION — For Radiant Revive's own customer intake photos, where crowdsourced labeling is not feasible, the ITA algorithm described here could programmatically estimate Fitzpatrick from patient-uploaded images as a fallback. This is a Phase 2 consideration.

SBIR/PATENT REFERENCE USE:
- Cite in SBIR Methods section on data preprocessing and label handling.
- Cite in Measurement Protocol future revisions justifying the dual-axis FST+MST stratification decision.
- Cite in any Radiant Revive publication discussing label reliability or annotation methodology.

SCOPE OF PRACTICE: Informs data curation methodology, not clinical treatment decisions.

library_docs.title: NeurIPS 2023 — Intrinsic Self-Supervision for Data Quality Audits (Gröger, Groh et al.)
library_docs.source: Gröger F, Lionetti S, Gottfrois P, Gonzalez-Jimenez A, Amruthalingam L, Labelling Consortium, Groh M, Navarini AA, Pouly M. Intrinsic self-supervision for data quality audits. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS). 2023. arXiv:2305.17048. Matt Groh, PhD (Northwestern Kellogg) contributor. Curated for Radiant Revive by Dr. Groh 2026-07-15.
library_docs.summary:
SELF-SUPERVISED METHODOLOGY for auditing image dataset quality (duplicates, near-duplicates, mislabels) without requiring additional human labels. Directly applicable to Radiant Revive's multi-source combined-corpus training approach.

KEY METHODOLOGICAL POINTS THE AI SHOULD APPLY:

1. NEAR-DUPLICATE DETECTION ACROSS DATASETS — The method identifies visually similar images that may exist across DDI + Fitzpatrick 17k + PAD-UFES-20 + SCIN. If the same clinical image appears in two datasets, using it in both training and validation would inflate accuracy estimates. This is a hidden risk in multi-source training.

2. MISLABEL DETECTION — Learns intrinsic representation of the data and flags samples whose labels are inconsistent with the intrinsic clusters. Would surface cases in Fitzpatrick 17k where the crowdsourced Fitzpatrick label disagrees with the image's actual skin-tone appearance.

3. NO HUMAN LABELS REQUIRED FOR THE AUDIT — Uses self-supervision, meaning the audit runs on raw image pixels without needing additional annotator time. Cost: pure GPU compute, roughly one training pass equivalent.

4. IMPLICATIONS FOR RADIANT REVIVE:
   - Add this as a Phase 1.3 PREPROCESSING STEP before combined-corpus training. Estimated 2-4 hours of GPU time to run across all four datasets.
   - Document the audit outcomes in the engineering log — creates defensible provenance for the training corpus.
   - Flag ANY detected duplicates in write-ups; explicitly state whether duplicates were dropped, kept-in-one-dataset-only, or included with weighted deduplication.

5. FAIRNESS IMPLICATIONS — Label noise is not evenly distributed across Fitzpatrick brackets. If mislabels concentrate in darker-skin subgroups (plausible given inter-rater reliability findings from Groh et al. 2022 CSCW), a naive training run would learn to under-predict on those brackets. The audit would surface this before it becomes a model-behavior problem.

6. GITHUB CODE AVAILABLE — The paper's replication code is public; the audit method can be integrated into Radiant Revive's Phase 1.3 pipeline as a standalone script or wrapped as a preprocessing module.

SBIR/PATENT REFERENCE USE:
- Cite in SBIR Methods section on data quality audits and rigorous preprocessing.
- Cite in any future publication on Radiant Revive's Phase 1.3 preprocessing pipeline.
- Cite as evidence of technical de-risking in the training corpus construction narrative.

SCOPE OF PRACTICE: Informs data engineering methodology, not clinical treatment decisions.

library_docs.source: Desir N, Encarnacion IN, Hamid A, Turner K, Oyasiji O, Elbuluk NM, Taylor SC. JAAD Reviews 2025;4:69-82. doi:10.1016/j.jdrv.2025.03.003. Open access CC BY-NC-ND. Susan C. Taylor, MD — University of Pennsylvania.
library_docs.summary:
DEFINITIVE 20-YEAR REVIEW of skin of color dermatology by the founder of the field (Dr. Susan Taylor, UPenn) and her team. Use this as the authoritative reference for any SOC question.

KEY CLINICAL POINTS THE AI SHOULD APPLY:

1. STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCES — Fitzpatrick V-VI clients have lower ceramide levels and higher protein cohesion in the stratum corneum. East Asian skin has increased trans-epidermal water loss. Prioritize ceramide-replenishing moisturizers (e.g. PCA ReBalance, PCA Hydraluxe) for IV-VI clients.

2. ATOPIC DERMATITIS — Highest prevalence in African Americans (19.3%). East Asian endotype is TH17/TH2 blended (AD-psoriasis crossover). African American endotype shows greater TH2 skewing and filaggrin variations.

3. PSORIASIS — Asian and Hispanic patients experience MORE SEVERE disease despite lower prevalence than White patients. VISIBLE trial (first SOC-exclusive psoriasis trial) showed guselkumab PASI-90 in 74% by week 16.

4. ACNE in SOC — More frequently causes hypertrophic/keloidal scarring and dyspigmentation. Topical dapsone gel = first-line. 1726 nm lasers (FDA 2022) safe and effective in Fitzpatrick II-VI for active acne. Energy-based scar treatments (Er:YAG, fractional CO2, picosecond) safe with cooling.

5. MELASMA — Non-hydroquinone options now well-validated in SOC: topical metformin 30% (= Kligman's formula), Thiamidol (isobutylamidol-thiazolyl resorcinol), tranexamic acid 5% cream (= 4% hydroquinone with fewer side effects), cysteamine 5% (= hydroquinone in multiple RCTs Fitzpatrick II-V), silymarin, Polypodium leucotomos. Lasers: 675-nm (II-III), 1064-nm QSNY.

6. POST-INFLAMMATORY HYPERPIGMENTATION (PIH) — Use PAHPI (Post-Acne Hyperpigmentation Index) for tracking; validated in skin type VI. Thiamidol safe/effective in Fitzpatrick II-V. 1927-nm laser effective IV-VI.

7. ACQUIRED DERMAL MACULAR HYPERPIGMENTATION (ADMH, 2017 umbrella term) — covers lichen planus pigmentosus, ashy dermatosis, Riehl's melanosis. Off-label options tested in SOC: topical tranexamic acid + topical ruxolitinib, oral tranexamic acid, oral isotretinoin, 1064-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG, picosecond laser.

8. COSMETIC SAFETY IN SOC — Validated safe in Fitzpatrick IV-VI: Botulinum toxin A, PrabotulinumtoxinA, AbobotulinumtoxinA, HA fillers, calcium hydroxyapatite fillers, poly-L-lactic acid. Lasers safe with cooling: Nd:YAG, pulsed-diode, pulsed-dye, thulium, alexandrite, radiofrequency + microneedling, microfocused laser. Older-generation lasers were contraindicated.

9. HAIR STRUCTURE — Black: elliptical curved follicles → curly, prone to knot/fissure. Curly/kinky hair has greater viscoelasticity and lower tensile strength. CROWN Act (2019) prohibits race-based hair discrimination (23 states).

10. SEBORRHEIC DERMATITIS — PETALOID SD more common in Fitzpatrick V-VI, can MIMIC SECONDARY SYPHILIS. Roflumilast 0.3% foam (PDE-4 inhibitor) treats SD and addresses post-inflammatory pigmentary changes — game-changer for SOC.

11. TRACTION ALOPECIA (TA) — Black, but also hijab-wearing women, turban-wearing Sikh men, ballet dancers, active-duty service women. FLAMBEAU SIGN (torch-like white tracts) = early trichoscopic finding in Black patients. Treatment: intralesional corticosteroids + topical/oral minoxidil. Scalp biopsy for unclear cases (Black women initially Dx as TA often have other/additional alopecia).

12. CENTRAL CENTRIFUGAL CICATRICIAL ALOPECIA (CCCA) — Predominately Black adult women; also pediatric, men, Native American women. May have NONVERTEX presentation. 2024 Delphi consensus: oral tetracycline + intralesional/topical corticosteroids. Comorbidities: uterine leiomyomas, type 2 diabetes, breast cancer (under investigation). Emerging: low-dose metformin, JAK inhibitors.

13. FRONTAL FIBROSING ALOPECIA — In Black patients, look for perifollicular hyperpigmentation along hairline + concomitant facial hyperpigmentation. Distinguish from TA.

14. ANDROGENETIC ALOPECIA — Low-dose oral minoxidil (0.25–5 mg daily) emerging safe/effective off-label. Trichoscopy critical to rule out scarring CCCA in men of African ancestry.

15. NAIL DISORDERS — Longitudinal melanonychia affects 70% of Fitzpatrick IV-VI. SINGLE-DIGIT LM WARRANTS MELANOMA EVALUATION — refer urgently. Micro-Hutchinson sign on dermoscopy = nail melanoma feature. Nail melanoma is 17-25% of all melanomas in SOC vs <5% in White populations. Significant disparities in Black/Hispanic later-stage presentation.

16. SBIR/AI DERMATOLOGY REFERENCE — The paper explicitly states: 'The integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning into diagnostic tools promises to revolutionize the ability to identify subtle variations in skin conditions across diverse skin types, reducing diagnostic delays and improving outcomes for SOC patients.' Cite this in any SBIR/grant Specific Aims section justifying SOC-focused AI dermatology research. Authored by THE founder of SOC dermatology.

SCOPE OF PRACTICE: This paper informs WHAT to refer and WHY. Niya is an RN providing wellness coaching, not dermatology diagnosis. Use as referral and education backbone — not as prescribing authority.

library_docs.title: Plantar Hyperkeratosis — Types, Causes, Diagnosis and Treatment (IU School of Medicine, Dermatology Clinical Trials)
library_docs.source: Indiana University School of Medicine, Department of Dermatology — Dermatology Clinical Trials. "What is Plantar Hyperkeratosis: Types, Causes & Treatment Options." Published 19 Nov 2024. https://dermatrials.medicine.iu.edu/blogs/what-is-plantar-hyperkeratosis [SOURCE TIER: institutional patient-education article, not peer-reviewed]
library_docs.summary: Reference summary (condensed; see source for full text). Plantar hyperkeratosis is epidermal thickening of the soles from keratin accumulation, typically at pressure-bearing sites such as the heels and balls of the feet. Contributing factors include repetitive friction and pressure (ill-fitting footwear, prolonged standing, running), genetic predisposition, elevated body weight, and underlying dermatoses such as psoriasis or eczema. Presentation: thickened plaques, pain on weight-bearing, peeling, and fissuring — fissures being a portal for secondary infection. Diagnosis is clinical (history plus examination of size, site and texture); biopsy is reserved for unclear cases to exclude other dermatoses. Management ladder: emollients and barrier repair; soaking with gentle exfoliation; topical keratolytics such as salicylic acid; debridement of thickened tissue in severe cases; surgical excision rarely. Prevention: properly fitted footwear, pressure offloading, weight management, and routine foot inspection. NOTE FOR DIFFERENTIAL USE: this source frames plantar thickening in mechanical and dermatologic terms only and does not address systemic causes. Bilateral involvement of BOTH soles and palms is not explained by plantar pressure and warrants a systemic workup independent of this reference.
